detailed_summary: The paper presents an exact computational classification of thermal-idle instruments in a quantum processor with ideal stabilizer control and independent local Markov baths. The authors show that the computational power of such a processor—whether it is classically simulable or quantum universal—depends on which environmental records the controller retains, even at fixed thermal exposure. The classification hinges on three parameters: the relaxation time T1, homogeneous coherence time T2, and equilibrium excited-state population pe. An exact boundary is derived at (1-pe)T2/T1 = 1. Below or at this boundary, branchwise nonnegative stabilizer decompositions yield an efficient classical sampler for the adaptive circuit and its full time-resolved exchange record. Above the boundary at a single repeatedly accessible location, a suitable idle duration and no-exchange conditioning enable distillable ancillas and universal quantum computation with polynomial overhead. The paper further explores finite-temperature resource states, showing that erasing the record at a sufficiently long, unsplit exposure makes the averaged channel stabilizer measure-and-prepare, rendering even a terminal parity check simulable. However, retaining only the bit recording whether any exchange occurred still heralds distillable ancillas, due to a thermal round trip restoring parity after the first exchange removes coherence.
key_contributions: Derivation of an exact computational boundary at (1-pe)T2/T1 = 1 that separates classically simulable from quantum universal behavior for thermal-idle instruments in stabilizer processors.
Construction of an explicit efficient classical sampler for adaptive circuits and their full time-resolved exchange records when all locations lie at or below the boundary.

Demonstration that above the boundary at a single repeatedly accessible location, distillable ancillas and universal quantum computation can be achieved with polynomial overhead via suitable idle duration and no-exchange conditioning.

Analysis of finite-temperature resource states: erasing the record at long, unsplit exposure makes the averaged channel stabilizer measure-and-prepare, but retaining only the bit of whether any exchange occurred still enables distillable ancillas.
Clarification of the role of environmental records in determining computational power, showing that the same physical processor can be either classical or quantum depending on record retention.
methodology_analysis: The authors employ an exact analytical approach based on stabilizer formalism and Markovian bath models. They consider a quantum processor with ideal stabilizer control and independent local Markov baths, characterized by T1, T2, and pe. The key methodological tool is branchwise nonnegative stabilizer decompositions, which allow them to construct an efficient classical sampler when the boundary condition is satisfied. For the quantum universal regime, they use no-exchange conditioning and idle duration to generate distillable ancillas. The analysis is exact, not approximate, and leverages the structure of thermal-idle instruments to classify computational power. The finite-temperature resource analysis involves examining the averaged channel and its stabilizer measure-and-prepare property, as well as the effect of retaining a single bit of exchange information.
results_analysis: The central result is the exact boundary at (1-pe)T2/T1 = 1. Below or at this boundary, the processor is classically simulable, and an explicit efficient classical sampler is provided for the adaptive circuit and its full time-resolved exchange record. Above the boundary at a single repeatedly accessible location, universal quantum computation is enabled with polynomial overhead. At finite temperature, erasing the record at a sufficiently long, unsplit exposure makes the averaged channel stabilizer measure-and-prepare, so even a terminal parity check yields only simulable branches. However, retaining only the bit recording whether any exchange occurred still heralds distillable ancillas, because a thermal round trip restores the parity after its first exchange has already removed the coherence. These results are exact and provide a sharp computational phase transition.
strengths: Provides an exact, analytical classification of computational power for a realistic noise model, with a clear boundary condition.
Introduces a novel perspective on the role of environmental records in determining quantum computational advantage.
Constructs explicit efficient classical samplers and universal quantum computation protocols, demonstrating practical implications.
The analysis is rigorous and self-contained, with clear physical interpretations of the parameters T1, T2, and pe.
limitations: Assumes ideal stabilizer control and independent local Markov baths, which may not hold in all experimental platforms.
The boundary condition is derived for a specific model of thermal-idle instruments; generalization to other noise models is not explored.
The resource analysis for finite-temperature states focuses on a specific scenario (retaining only the exchange bit) and may not cover all possible record-retention strategies.
connections_to_research: This work is directly relevant to quantum physics, particularly in the areas of quantum computation, quantum error correction, and open quantum systems. It addresses fundamental questions about the boundary between classical and quantum computational power in the presence of noise, which is central to understanding quantum advantage. The use of stabilizer formalism and Markovian baths connects to quantum information theory and the study of decoherence. The results have implications for the design of quantum processors and the role of environmental monitoring in quantum algorithms.
overall_assessment: The paper is a significant contribution to the theory of quantum computation under noise. It provides a sharp, exact boundary for classical simulability versus quantum universality in a realistic model, and highlights the subtle role of environmental records. The novelty lies in the exact classification and the counterintuitive result that retaining a single bit of information can enable quantum advantage even when the averaged channel is classical. The work is rigorous and well-motivated, though its assumptions may limit direct applicability. Overall, it is a high-quality theoretical study that advances our understanding of the quantum-classical transition in noisy processors.
